name: PT Mora Telematika Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ekamas Mora Republik — a national fibre build the share price still does not pay for
frontmatter.summary: Moratelindo merged with MyRepublic Indonesia in April 2026 and became one of the country's largest fibre-to-the-home footprints by homepass, but the deal doubled the share count, tripled the debt and left the equity behind a build that consumes all of operating cash flow. Our DCF puts fundamental value at Rp125; the concentration lens keeps part of the premium and still lands below the price. Initiate at SELL, target Rp1,000.
thesis: The merger changed the company more than the price reflects in either direction - it is now a retail FTTH operator with a national access network, not the wholesale backbone business the last audited accounts describe.

On our cash-flow work the merged business is worth a fraction of the market capitalisation; the gap is a float and flow premium, not an earnings premium, and the concentration lens only keeps part of it over twelve months.
The build is debt-funded and dividend-free, so the equity is a levered bet on homepass monetisation at a time when Indonesian fixed-broadband ARPU is under pressure.
The governance profile is the Sinar Mas group's - a related-party asset injection, a high-shareholding-concentration listing and a free float sitting on the regulatory minimum.
What would change the view is evidence of take-up and capex discipline - net additions, ARPU and capex-to-revenue - not a lower share price.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: first full year of the merged entity, homepass and subscriber additions against the 2026 plan
MSCI consultation feedback window closes on the proposed move of Indonesia to Standalone status
MSCI decision on Indonesian market classification
Annual general meeting: dividend resolution and board renewal

blocks.text: We initiate PT Ekamas Mora Republik Tbk — the company formerly listed as PT Mora Telematika Indonesia, ticker MORA — at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp1,000, -37.3% from the Rp1,595 last traded. The target is not our fundamental value: it is the engine's most-likely twelve-month price for a concentrated-ownership name, which keeps part of the gap between the price and what the business is worth. Our fundamental twelve-month value is Rp125; the price sits at 14.4 times our current fundamental value of Rp111 [S0].

The company is no longer the business its last audited accounts describe. In April 2026 Moratelindo absorbed PT Eka Mas Republik, the Indonesian arm of MyRepublic, and renamed itself; the merged group is one of the largest fibre-to-the-home footprints in the country by homepass, with 12,700,000.0 homepass and 2,600,000.0 subscribers [S5]. The transaction was settled in shares, diluting pre-merger holders by 50.5 per cent [S3], and it brought a network, a retail subscriber base and a large debt stack onto the balance sheet at once [S0].

What the market pays for that is a market capitalisation of IDR76,199.8bn against a business that generated IDR1,875.3bn of EBITDA in its last audited year before the merger [S0, S6]. The share price has already fallen a long way from its Rp15,775 high to Rp1,595 [S0], and it is still priced for a cash-flow stream the company does not yet produce: our reverse DCF says today's price needs revenue growth of roughly 54.2% on top of our forecast in every year of the horizon, which is beyond anything the merger plan implies [S0].

Three things move the value. First, take-up: the merged footprint is only about a fifth penetrated, so net additions and ARPU decide whether the network earns its cost of capital [S5, S6]. Second, capex: the company plans to add five million homepass in 2026 alone and guides capital spending up by a double-digit percentage, which is why free cash flow is negative and debt is rising [S5, S6]. Third, the regime: the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, on which the merged company is named [S10], and the MSCI consultation on Indonesia's market status mean the marginal buyer is a flow, not a fundamental investor, and that is exactly what the lens in the valuation section prices [S9].

We are not bearish because the price fell. We are bearish because the arithmetic of a debt-funded fibre build at this valuation does not work, and because the most likely path for a name like this — a partial, slow closing of an extreme premium — still leaves the shares below today's price.

Moratelindo was founded in 2000 and listed in 2022 as a wholesale connectivity business: domestic and international backhaul, internet exchange and IP transit, a network access point business selling to other operators, enterprise connectivity, and a small portfolio of data centres [S6, S7]. Its customers were telcos, internet service providers, corporates, government bodies and buildings, not households. The retail arm, sold under the Oxygen brand, was a minority of the business [S6].

The FY2025 operating statistics describe that company: six data centres running at a utilisation rate in the high seventies, several hundred points of presence, a domestic and submarine fibre network of tens of thousands of kilometres, and a fibre-to-the-home footprint of just over a million homepass with 330,710.0 subscribers on it [S6]. The revenue mix is the one the segment note reports: retail and enterprise together 33.5% of revenue, wholesale 21.9%, the telco operator segment the balance of the connectivity lines, and a large "other" line of IDR1,225.7bn that is construction revenue and the finance income on the Palapa Ring West service concession rather than a customer business [S6]. Retail and enterprise is therefore the largest single customer-facing segment, and it is the one the merger multiplies [S6].

That shape changed on 22 April 2026, when the merger with PT Eka Mas Republik became effective and the surviving entity was renamed PT Ekamas Mora Republik Tbk [S5, S7]. The transaction was agreed in December 2025, cleared by the financial services authority in March 2026 and completed in April [S7, S3]. MyRepublic brought a retail FTTH business built since 2015, with a homepass count that had grown from a few hundred thousand to more than ten million by 2025 [S5]. On the company's own numbers the merged group starts with 12,700,000.0 homepass and more than 2,600,000.0 subscribers [S5].

The strategic logic the company gives is scale: a combined access network, cross-selling between the wholesale backbone and the retail base, and a single build programme across more cities [S4, S5]. Management's 2026 plan is explicit — add 5,000,000 homepass, add 1,500,000 subscribers, and extend to a much larger set of cities and regencies [S5]. Capital expenditure is guided up by a double-digit percentage against the prior year, and the company expects EBITDA to grow by a double-digit percentage too [S6].

The group behind it is Sinar Mas. Eka Mas Republik sat under the group before the merger, the transaction was announced by the group's listed holding company, and the group emerges as the majority holder of the merged entity [S3]. That makes MORA the group's listed fibre and data-centre vehicle alongside its other listed companies, and it makes the merger a related-party transaction rather than an arm's-length acquisition — a point we return to in the governance section.
The company employs 1,719 people [S0]. It reports in rupiah and its financial year ends in December.

Indonesian fixed broadband has historically been a small part of the connectivity market relative to mobile, with household penetration well below mobile penetration and a long tail of small local operators alongside the national incumbents. Fibre-to-the-home economics depend on homepass density, take-up and ARPU; operators that build ahead of demand carry the financing cost until subscribers arrive. Data-centre demand in the region has grown with cloud adoption, and Jakarta has been the concentrated hub.

Indonesian internet demand is large and still growing. The internet service providers' association reported penetration of about four-fifths of the population with an estimated user base in the hundreds of millions, and peak internet-exchange traffic at the Jakarta exchange point reached double-digit terabits per second in 2025 [S6]. The company's own reading of the market is that data growth, cloud adoption and digitalisation are pulling through demand for backbone, FTTH, network access points and data centres simultaneously [S6].

The fixed-broadband segment is where the merger changes the competitive map. The company describes a market with several national and regional FTTH operators competing for household connections, and it names ARPU pressure and intensifying competition as the defining industry conditions of 2025 [S6]. That is the base rate for Indonesian data pricing: capacity is built ahead of demand, operators compete on speed and price, and realised revenue per user falls even as volumes rise [S6]. The merged entity is now one of the largest FTTH footprints by homepass, but homepass is a build metric, not a revenue metric — the value depends on converting it [S5]. Run the arithmetic the way the company reports it: the retail and enterprise segment earned IDR1,340.3bn in FY2025, 33.5% of group revenue, on 330,000 retail customers and 17,000 enterprise customers [S6, S5], and the merged group starts with 2,600,000.0 subscribers on 12,700,000.0 homepass [S5]. Revenue per subscriber is therefore the number to watch, and it is the one a price war moves first.

Data centres are the second leg. The company operates a small portfolio at high utilisation, and the Indonesian data-centre market is described in its own annual report as growing quickly but still concentrated in Jakarta [S6]. That is a genuine growth option, but it is small relative to the access network and it competes with far larger regional operators.

Regulation cuts two ways. On the demand side, the government's digital agenda and the universal-service framework support network build-out, and the company pays a universal-service obligation charge that sits in its direct costs [S6]. On the market side, the exchange has raised the minimum free float and tightened ownership disclosure, and MSCI is consulting on moving Indonesia to standalone status because it judged the reforms insufficient to address opaque ownership and suspected coordinated trading [S9]. For a company named on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S10], that is a structural constraint on the buyer base, not a temporary sentiment.

Five forces, briefly. Rivalry is high and price-based: several FTTH operators chase the same households and ARPU is falling [S6]. Buyer power is high because switching costs for a household are low and contracts are short. Supplier power is moderate — fibre and equipment are competitive, but backhaul and content are concentrated. New entrants are a real threat in dense urban areas where overbuilding is cheap, which is why homepass counts in Jakarta and Surabaya are worth less than the headline. Substitutes include fixed wireless and mobile data, which cap what a household will pay for a fixed line.

The moat is the physical network: ducts, poles, submarine landing capacity and a national backbone are expensive and slow to replicate, and the company's infrastructure business rents that asset to other operators [S6]. That is a real advantage in wholesale. In retail FTTH it is weaker, because the last mile into a housing estate can be overbuilt and the customer can switch. Our view is that the wholesale and data-centre businesses earn a return above the cost of capital and the retail access business, at current ARPU, does not yet.
The macro deck matters mainly through rates: the company is a leveraged infrastructure borrower, so the policy-rate path and the rupiah set its refinancing cost and its discount rate [S0].

The last audited year is the pre-merger company. FY2025 revenue was IDR4,000.2bn, up 0.6% on FY2024, with a gross margin of 59.2% and EBITDA of IDR1,875.3bn on our restated basis [S6]. The company itself reports a higher EBITDA figure for the year, up nearly a tenth, and net profit of IDR515.9bn, which nearly doubled as financing costs fell after the sukuk ijarah was repaid [S6]. Net profit attributable to shareholders was IDR448.5bn [S6].

One restatement matters. The data pack carries depreciation and amortisation of a small fraction of the real charge, because Indonesian filings use the direct cash-flow method and the D&A sits in the notes rather than on the face of the cash-flow statement. The notes show depreciation of property and equipment of IDR765.4bn for FY2025, split between direct costs and operating expenses, plus right-of-use depreciation and intangible amortisation on top [S6]. We restate the line to the note figure, which lifts EBITDA from the pack's figure to IDR1,875.3bn and is the difference between a business that looks like it earns a margin in the thirties and one that earns one in the high forties [S6].

Cash generation is the weak point. Operating cash flow was IDR1,525.9bn in FY2025 while capital expenditure on property and equipment was IDR1,324.1bn, so free cash flow to the firm was IDR-119.2bn before any growth capex [S6]. The company funded the gap with debt: net debt stood at IDR3,979.5bn at the end of FY2025, or 2.1 times EBITDA [S0, S6].

FY2026 is not comparable. The merger consolidated a much larger asset base and a much larger debt stack from late April, and the September balance sheet carries a debt stack several times the pre-merger level because the merger brought MyRepublic borrowings with it [S0]. Revenue for the nine months to September was already above the whole of FY2025, which is why our FY2026E growth rate of 82.0% is a consolidation effect and not organic growth [S0, S5]. We forecast FY2026E revenue of IDR7,280.4bn and EBITDA of IDR3,713.0bn.

*Note to the leverage row: it divides the model's roll net debt, which carries no line for the share-funded merger and so is not the leverage the company has. On the 30 September 2026 balance sheet debt is IDR17,861.9bn against FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,713.0bn and FY2027E EBITDA of IDR4,872.3bn [S0], and our DCF deducts that actual debt, not the roll. The balance-sheet artefact is explained below.*

Our forecast logic is deliberately plain. The 32.0% revenue step in FY2027E is not organic growth and the report should not read as if it were: MyRepublic contributed eight months of 2026, so FY2027E carries twelve, and against the third quarter's annualised rate the step-up is high single digits — in line with the company's own pre-merger guidance of a single-digit increase and with a market where ARPU is falling [S0, S6]. We hold the gross margin at 61.0%, the level the merged business already prints, and we hold operating costs at 36.5% of revenue for the whole forecast, above the standalone company's ratio because retail FTTH carries a heavier selling and service load [S0, S4]. We do not bank the merger's duplicate-cost savings in the base case: they are a management claim without an audited result, so they sit in the bull scenario and the base case holds the merged ratio flat [S4].

Depreciation is the swing item. The merged property and equipment base is several times the standalone one, and at the depreciation rate the FY2025 notes imply that is a charge of roughly a quarter of revenue, which we carry at 26.2% [S6, S0]. That is what turns a high-forties EBITDA margin into an operating margin in the twenties and a net margin only in the low double digits once interest is paid.

Capex is the reason the equity is not free cash flow. Nine-month 2026 capital spending was almost all of nine-month revenue — inflated by bringing the MyRepublic access network onto the balance sheet — and the company guides 2026 spending up by a double-digit percentage with a homepass target of 5,000,000 additions [S0, S5, S6]. We model capex at 78.0% of revenue in FY2026E — the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the first-half quarterly average, because the third quarter carried the consolidation step — falling to 40.0% in FY2027E and to 29.0% by FY2030E, where it stays [S0, S5, S6]. That last number matters, and it is deliberately above the 25.5% D&A charge rather than equal to it. A network whose capex only replaces depreciation does not grow, so a terminal value that grows revenue at 4.5% in perpetuity while spending only D&A leaves the growth unfunded and overstates terminal free cash flow. The gap is the growth times capital intensity: at a net fixed-asset base of about IDR15,124.5bn on revenue of IDR12,105.0bn, terminal growth needs roughly four points of revenue in net investment on top of replacement, which is why capex settles at 29.0% against D&A of 25.5% [S0]. The first draft set terminal capex below D&A, which implied a network shrinking in perpetuity; the second set it equal to D&A, which funded replacement but not growth. Both are corrected [S0].

Financing follows from that, and it is the part of the first draft that was wrong. The merger put IDR17,861.9bn of debt on the balance sheet at 30 September 2026 against IDR5,345.3bn at the prior year-end, and a full year of interest on that stack is IDR982.4bn, not the IDR294.0bn the engine books for FY2026E [S0]. The forecast books the acquired debt in FY2026E, so debt stands at the actual IDR17,861.9bn and FY2027E interest is struck on a full year of it, at the 5.5% cash rate the September quarter actually paid, annualised [S0].

FY2026E interest needs saying precisely, because the engine's convention is not a stub. The engine charges the rate on the *opening* balance, and FY2026E opens on the pre-merger IDR5,345.3bn stack, so the IDR294.0bn shown is a full year of interest on the smaller, older debt — it carries none of the debt consolidated on 22 April 2026 [S0, S5]. The merger-period charge on the right split — four months on the standalone stack and eight on the merged one — is materially higher than that, and the difference is booked in other non-operating items for FY2026E so that the year's profit before tax is struck on the financing the company actually carried [S0, S5]. FY2026E is a consolidated stub in every other respect too, and we do not lean on its earnings: the year that matters for the rating is FY2027E, where the balance sheet and the interest are both the merged ones.

One residual has to be stated plainly, because it sits behind two lines of the table above. The engine's annual roll has no line for a share-funded acquisition: it books the acquired debt but not the share issue that paid for the assets, so every rupiah of that debt also lands in the cash line. The model therefore carries IDR12,344.3bn of cash in FY2026E against the IDR1,365.8bn it opened with, and its net-debt line is far below the balance the company actually carries. Two consequences are handled explicitly rather than buried. First, interest income: the model is charged interest only on the cash the balance sheet really holds. FY2027E interest income is IDR46.9bn, in line with the IDR47.9bn the standalone company earned and with what the September cash earns at the rate it is paid, rather than the multiple of it that a nominal yield on the roll's cash would produce [S0]. FY2026E is the mirror image — the same adjusted yield on a real opening balance understates that year's interest income — and the effect is small and already inside the FY2026E financing correction, so no third adjustment is made. Second, the leverage row: as the note under the table says, that line divides the roll and is not the company's leverage — on the actual 30 September 2026 debt the company carries several times the multiple the row shows [S0]. We state the row's defect rather than adjust capex to hide it, because charging a share-funded acquisition against free cash flow would double-count the dilution, and the valuation is unaffected: it deducts the actual net debt, not the roll [S0]. The share count is the enlarged one throughout — 47,766 million shares after the issue of a further half of the company to the vendor [S3, S0].

Capital allocation is unambiguous: no dividend, no policy on dividends, and a resolution at the 2025 annual meeting not to pay one on the prior year's profit [S6]. Every rupiah of operating cash flow goes back into the network. That is defensible for a company in a build phase, but it means the equity has no income support and no buyback floor. On the debt: the FY2025 accounts show bank facilities with BRI, Permata, BCA and the regional banks, and the two sukuk tranches that matured in May and July 2025 were repaid from cash [S6 p.123, p.284]; the post-merger stack is bank debt and the FY2025 notes do not describe it, so the refinancing calendar is a monitoring item rather than a modelled date. That gap is itself a risk: debt trebled in three quarters and we cannot yet see the maturity wall [S0].

Earnings quality. The accruals picture is clean — operating cash flow exceeds net profit, so earnings are backed by cash [S6]. Two flags are worth stating. First, receivables grew much faster than revenue in FY2025, and inventory grew while direct costs fell, which is the kind of divergence the house screen looks for even when the absolute amounts are small [S0]. Second, the company carries a large fixed-asset revaluation surplus from a PSAK 16 revaluation, which inflates book value and flatters any price-to-book comparison; we do not use book value in the valuation [S6]. Neither is a manipulation-class flag. Both are disclosed.

We value MORA on discounted cash flow as the primary method, with the AFFO-yield test as the cross-check the industry card requires. That set fits the asset: a long-lived network with a defined build cycle, a leveraged balance sheet and a regulated-adjacent revenue base is a cash-flow business, and a multiple applied to a merger-stub LTM is a weak anchor. We carry the EV/EBITDA leg at zero weight for the D&A reason set out below, not because multiples are unwelcome; the AFFO yield against the ten-year bond does the same job with a metric built from the restated accounts.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.85 for a fibre and data-centre operator, levered to 1.01 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.23, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%. That 0.23 is the market ratio: the engine divides the debt by the market capitalisation, and the market capitalisation here carries a multiple of fundamental value, so the ratio is far below the company's book or fundamental gearing. The choice is stated rather than buried because it is the conservative one — at a fundamental debt-to-equity the levered beta, the cost of equity and the weights would all be lower and the WACC lower with them, which is the direction of the lower-WACC columns in the sensitivity table [S0]. We keep the market ratio because it is the one a marginal buyer of the equity actually faces today, and because a company whose price is a float premium should not also be handed a cheaper discount rate. The cost-of-equity bridge is explicit: the rupiah ten-year yield of 7.4% less the 1.6% default spread the engine deducts to reach a sovereign-risk-free rate, plus 1.01 times the mature premium, plus the country premium — a cost of equity of 12.6% and a WACC of 11.6% [S0]. The spread deduction is the difference between the bond yield a saver receives and the risk-free rate a valuation needs, and it is large here because the rupiah yield is high and the credit is investment grade; without it the cost of equity would be overstated by that spread.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR20,047.8bn and a value per share of Rp70, with the terminal value accounting for 59.0% of the total [S0]. The terminal value share is high but not extreme for a network business; the sensitivity table shows what happens if the WACC or the terminal growth assumption is wrong.

We do not carry an EV/EBITDA leg in the blend, and the reason is the restatement above, not a preference for the DCF. The engine's multiple is applied to last-twelve-month EBITDA taken from the data pack, which is IDR1,109.9bn of EBIT plus a fraction of the true depreciation — the same understated-D&A problem the restatement corrects. The own-history multiple is struck on that same understated history, so it is inflated by roughly the ratio by which the restatement lifts EBITDA. Applying an inflated multiple to a deflated metric almost cancels, which is why the leg printed close to the DCF under the old weights and why quoting it as an independent cross-check would be false precision. On a restated EBITDA the corrected history multiple falls to the high single digits; applied to our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,713.0bn that implies an enterprise value well above the DCF's IDR20,047.8bn, and it is not a number we can defend as a cross-check. The multiple was earned on a standalone asset base that earned it with under a third of today's debt and about half today's revenue; a merger-stub year carrying a pre-merger multiple is not a valuation of the merged company. The leg therefore adds no information in either direction and is set to zero weight, disclosed here rather than dropped silently [S0, S6].

The AFFO test is the one the industry card requires, and the honest answer is that it depends on which interest rate is used — so we show both rather than pick the flattering one. AFFO is EBITDA less maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax; maintenance capex is taken at the D&A charge of IDR2,517.9bn, because the company does not split maintenance from growth spending. On FY2027E that gives EBITDA of IDR4,872.3bn less D&A, less cash interest, plus interest income of IDR46.9bn, less cash tax of IDR340.6bn — which is our FY2027E net profit of IDR1,078.4bn, since maintenance capex equal to D&A and no working-capital build leave the two identical in this structure.

Two interest rates are in play and the gap between them is not an error. The 5.5% we charge in the P&L is the cash rate the company paid in the September quarter on its existing bank facilities, annualised [S0]; the 9.4% in the WACC is the marginal cost of *new* debt from the macro deck, the rupiah risk-free rate plus the corporate spread, because that is the rate at which the next rupiah of the build is financed. AFFO is a cash measure, so it is struck on the 5.5% actually paid; the WACC is a forward discount rate, so it carries the 9.4% marginal rate. Charging AFFO at the marginal rate instead would cut it to the region of half, and the test's verdict would not change: on either rate, the AFFO yield at our fundamental value of Rp125 — an equity value of that price times 47,766 million shares — is well above the 7.4% ten-year yield, and at the market price of Rp1,595 it is far below it. The conclusion of the first draft, that the AFFO yield does not clear the bond, was wrong and is withdrawn; the conclusion of the second, that it clears unconditionally, was right only because we had not said which rate we used. Stated this way, the test supports the direction of the DCF — the market price pays for cash flows the business does not generate — without depending on the interest-rate choice [S0].

What the price implies is the cleanest way to state the gap. Running the model backwards, today's Rp1,595 requires revenue growth of about 54.2% on top of our forecast in every year of the horizon — a rate the company has never sustained and that the merger plan does not claim [S0, S5]. This is a *fundamental* test: it asks what a cash-flow buyer would have to believe. It is not evidence about what sets the price today — that is the lens, and the two explanations are alternatives, not a joint proof. On the lens reading the price is not a discount rate on our cash flows at all; it is a float premium, and the reverse DCF simply measures how far that premium sits from anything the business generates [S9].

The concentration lens then does the regime step, and it is deliberately separate from the business work. The price sits at 14.4 times our current fundamental value of Rp111, against a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp125. The lens keeps part of that premium over twelve months, with the share kept set by the name's flags — high-shareholding-concentration status on the exchange's list, a free float on the regulatory minimum, and the 2026 regime against concentrated-ownership names [S10, S9]. In the base regime scenario the target is Rp706, in the bear case Rp243 and in the bull case Rp2,344, and the probability-weighted result is our Rp1,000 target [S0]. The lens is not a view that the premium is justified; it is a view about how fast a float-driven price converges, and for this name the honest answer is slowly.

The largest downside risk is the one the industry method card names first: a price war in Indonesian data. Fixed-broadband ARPU is already under pressure and the merged company is now much more exposed to retail pricing than it was [S6]. If realised ARPU falls faster than subscribers grow, revenue growth stalls while the network cost is already sunk. Likelihood high, impact high.

The second is capex and leverage. The company is spending ahead of demand and funding the gap with debt: the September balance sheet carries IDR17,861.9bn of debt against FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,713.0bn and FY2027E EBITDA of IDR4,872.3bn, cash of only a fraction of that debt, and a multiple that leaves no room for a build overrun; the quarterly interest bill has already stepped up to the run-rate we model [S0]. A delay in converting homepass to subscribers or a rise in the refinancing rate hits the equity, not the enterprise. Likelihood medium, impact high.

The third is integration, and the fourth is take-up. The merger closed in April and the two businesses had different customer bases, systems and cost structures; the synergy case is a management claim, not yet an audited result [S4, S5]. On take-up the arithmetic is unforgiving: the merged group starts with 12,700,000.0 homepass and 2,600,000.0 subscribers, a penetration of about a fifth, against the 1,075,581.0 homepass and 330,710.0 subscribers the standalone business ran — roughly three tenths — before the merger [S5, S6]. The company's 2026 plan is to add 1,500,000 subscribers [S5]. If it does, our base revenue path is too low; if ARPU falls as it has, even hitting the target may not lift revenue, because the retail and enterprise segment earned IDR1,340.3bn on 330,000 retail customers and 17,000 enterprise customers — the revenue per customer that a price war attacks directly [S6, S5]. We do not disclose a top-three customer share because the company does not: neither the annual report nor the merger disclosure gives customer concentration for the enterprise and wholesale book, which carries 17,000 enterprise customers and no single-customer disclosure. That is a monitoring gap on a wholesale business whose anchor tenants are telcos, and we treat it as a governance risk rather than a modelled one [S6, S5].

The fifth is regulatory and index. The exchange's free-float rule and the MSCI consultation on Indonesia's status are dated, binary events for the buyer base [S9]. A Standalone decision would remove the name from the emerging-market universe entirely. Likelihood medium, impact high on the price, low on the business.

The sixth is governance. The merger was a related-party asset injection by the controlling group, the company carries a revaluation surplus, and the float is thin [S3, S6]. Related-party terms are the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange. Likelihood low-to-medium, impact high.

The seventh is liquidity. Average daily traded value is IDR1.4bn and the free float is 15.8% [S0]. An institution cannot build or exit a position without moving the price, which is why the engine applies a liquidity discount of 10.0% to the fundamental value.

Our business scenarios are mirrored and tied to the take-up path the red team asked for. The bear case (25%) is a price war: the company misses its subscriber target, realised ARPU falls, revenue growth runs five percentage points below base, the gross margin gives up a point and a half and opex takes a point and a half more of revenue. The bull case (25%) is the company's own plan delivered: 1,500,000 net additions on the merged base, penetration moving from the merged rate toward the standalone rate, five points more growth, a point and a half more gross margin and the duplicate-cost savings the merger was sold on. The base case (50%) is the most probable path, not a cautious one: it assumes the company hits its build plan, converts homepass at the rate the merged footprint already shows rather than at the better standalone rate, and earns the margin the merged business already prints [S0, S5]. Because a levered builder in a price war can lose the equity, the bear scenario floors at zero — that is the arithmetic of the capital structure, not a forecast that the business disappears [S0].

The regime scenarios are separate from the business scenarios, and the split matters for how a reader should use the target. On the business work the value is Rp139; the price is 14.4 times the current fundamental value of Rp111, and over twelve months the lens keeps part of that gap, with the share kept set by the high-shareholding-concentration listing, the float sitting on the regulatory minimum and the 2026 enforcement and index regime [S10]. The bear regime closes most of the gap and lands at Rp243, the base case closes part of it at Rp706, and the bull case keeps the premium and lands at Rp2,344 [S0, S9]. A Standalone decision by MSCI, or the exchange widening its concentration list, would push the distribution toward the bear regime; a group transaction that lifted the float materially would do the opposite. Their catalysts are dated: the MSCI feedback window closes at the end of April 2027 and the classification decision is due by the end of June 2027 [S9]; the exchange reviews its concentration list quarterly; and the free-float deadlines run through 2027 and 2028 [S9].

Signposts that would change our view: net subscriber additions running ahead of the plan for two consecutive quarters; ARPU stabilising rather than falling; capex-to-revenue falling faster than we model without a slowdown in net adds; a dividend policy being adopted; or a group transaction that injects cash rather than assets.

MORA is a Sinar Mas group company. The Widjaja family's group controls the entity, Eka Mas Republik was a group asset before it was merged in, and the transaction was announced by the group's listed holding company [S3]. The merger is therefore the dominant related-party event of the period: the company issued shares equal to about half of the enlarged capital to acquire a business from its own controlling group, 50.5 per cent dilution to existing holders, at a valuation struck while its own shares were trading at an extreme premium [S3, S0]. Quantify what can be quantified: the shares handed to the vendor, valued at the Rp15,775 the market paid in the year before the deal, are a very large multiple of the EBITDA the entire merged group now produces [S0]. What cannot be quantified is what the group received: neither the merger disclosure nor the annual report states Eka Mas Republik's revenue or EBITDA at acquisition, so the implied multiple on the injected asset is not calculable from any source we can cite [S3, S5, S6]. That asymmetry — a price observable, the asset's earnings not — is exactly why the bear case carries the merger as a value-transfer risk and why we treat the equity story as a group capital-markets story as much as an operating one. We do not allege that the terms were unfair; the dilution was disclosed and approved.

That ownership structure is what the lens in the valuation section prices, and the konglo table is the evidence for it: a controlling family stake, a free float on the regulatory minimum, and a place on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which takes the shares out of the main indices and leaves the marginal buyer a flow rather than a fundamental investor [S10]. With the price at 14.4 times our current fundamental value of Rp111, the question the lens asks is not whether the premium is deserved — it is not — but what share of it survives twelve months when the float, the index status and the group's own capital-markets agenda set the price. The base case closes 35.0% of the log gap, the bear case closes 75.0% of it and the bull case keeps the premium and lets it re-expand; that is how a target above our fundamental value is consistent with a sell rating [S10, S0].

The float is the constraint. Free float is 15.8% against a regulatory minimum that the exchange has raised, and the company is named on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which takes it out of the main indices [S10, S0]. The 2026 regime has turned against exactly this kind of ownership: MSCI froze index increases for Indonesian securities, is consulting on Standalone status, and cited opaque ownership structures and suspected coordinated trading as its reasons [S9]. None of that is a finding of wrongdoing against MORA, and the company is compliant with the float rule; it is a statement about who can own the shares and at what price.

On the other governance items: the company has never paid a dividend and has no dividend policy, with the annual meeting resolving against a distribution on the prior year's profit [S6]. The FY2025 accounts are audited and the interim accounts are not, which is normal for the exchange but means the merger-period numbers we rely on for the current balance sheet are unaudited [S7]. The company carries a PSAK 16 revaluation surplus on property and equipment, which we strip out of any book-value work [S6]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the annual report; the concentration risk here is ownership, not margin loans.

ESG exposures are the ordinary ones for the sector: the energy intensity of data centres and network operations, electronic waste from customer premises equipment, and the social value of extending connectivity to underserved areas, which is also the company's growth story [S6]. Labour is small relative to the asset base. We do not see an ESG exposure that changes the valuation.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027, which will be the first clean read on the merged business and on whether the homepass and subscriber targets were met [S5]; the MSCI consultation feedback closing at the end of April 2027 and the classification decision by the end of June 2027 [S9]; the exchange's quarterly review of its concentration list; and the 2027 annual meeting, where the dividend question returns [S6].

Between updates we watch four numbers [S0]. Net subscriber additions against homepass added — the conversion rate is the whole thesis. Realised ARPU, because a falling ARPU with rising volumes is how this industry destroys returns. Capex as a share of revenue, because the path from the current build level to a maintenance level is what makes the DCF work or not. And reported net debt to EBITDA, because the equity is the residual of a leveraged structure and the refinancing calendar is the tail risk.
We will revisit the rating on any of the signposts above, and we will re-underwrite the model when the FY2026 accounts give us a full year of merged financials rather than a stub [S0].

bear.narrative: The FTTH price war wins: realised ARPU falls and net additions stall well short of the company's 2026 target, so revenue growth runs 5pp below base, the gross margin gives up 1.5pp and opex takes 1.5pp more of revenue while the homepass build continues at full cost [S6 p.27].

bull.narrative: Take-up follows the company's own 2026 plan - 1.5m net subscriber additions on a 2.6m merged base, with penetration moving from the merged 20.5% toward the 30.7% the standalone business already ran - so revenue growth runs 5pp above base, the gross margin gains 1.5pp and the duplicate-cost synergies land, taking 1.5pp off opex [S5 F21, F22; S6 p.18].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the merger year, not organic growth: MyRepublic Indonesia was consolidated from the 22 April 2026 effective date (S5) and nine-month revenue reached Rp 5.0trn against Rp 4.0trn for all of FY2025 (S0; the Rp 6.2trn twelve-month figure is LTM, not the nine-month period), so the full year is about 1.8x the standalone base. FY2027E carries the annualisation of the merged base (Q3 2026 alone ran at Rp 2.2trn, S0) - +32% against the stub year is the full-year effect of an acquisition that contributed eight months in 2026, not organic growth; against the Q3 annualised rate the step-up is high single digits, in line with the company's pre-merger single-digit guidance (S6 p.135) and with falling FTTH ARPU (S6 p.27).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine months of 2026 (revenue Rp 5.0trn, not the Rp 6.2trn twelve-month figure) already print a gross margin of 61% on the merged base (S0) against 59.2% standalone in FY2025 (S6 p.14); the wholesale/backbone mix and the removal of duplicate backhaul keep it at 61%. No margin expansion is assumed beyond that.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The merged retail FTTH business carries a heavier sales and marketing load: opex was 36.5% of revenue over nine months of 2026 (Rp 1.8trn on Rp 5.0trn, S0) and 38.8% in Q3 alone, against 31.2% for standalone MORA in FY2025 (S6 p.14). The base case holds the ratio at the merged actual, flat: the duplicate-function savings the merger was justified on (S4) are a management claim, not an audited result, so they sit in the bull case, not here.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Property and equipment reached Rp 27.4trn at September 2026 after consolidating MyRepublic (S0); FY2025 depreciation was 9.2% of average PPE (S6 note 13), which on the merged asset base is roughly Rp 2.5trn a year, about 26% of a full-year merged revenue base.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 capex of Rp 4.7trn equalled 93.7% of nine-month revenue of Rp 5.0trn because the merger brought the MyRepublic access network onto the balance sheet (S0); FY2025 standalone capex was 33.1% of revenue (Rp 1,324.1bn on Rp 4,000.2bn, S6 p.249 - the pack's 1,385.6 is the Yahoo figure) and the company guides 2026 capex up double digits (S6 p.135) with a target of five million new homepass in 2026 (S5). FY2026E therefore carries 78% of revenue - the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the first-half quarterly average, because Q3 carried the consolidation step (S0). The ratio then falls as the homepass build matures to 29%, NOT to the 25% D&A rate: at a 4.5% terminal growth rate a network whose capex equals its depreciation stops growing, so replacement capex must exceed D&A by growth x capital intensity (4.5% x net PPE/revenue of 0.94 = 4.2pp). Capex at 29% of revenue and D&A at 25% is internally consistent with terminal growth and funds no perpetual shrinkage.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Post-merger the merged balance sheet carries current liabilities close to current assets - operating working capital of Rp 0.24trn on Rp 6.2trn of LTM revenue, 3.9% (S0) - so 4% of revenue replaces the standalone 42% the engine measured on the pre-merger pack.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 effective rate was 24.0% (tax Rp 162.8bn on pre-tax Rp 678.6bn, S6 p.14) and the Q3 2026 quarter ran at 22%; 24% is the statutory rate the company actually pays.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Q3 2026 interest expense of Rp 239bn on Rp 17.9trn of debt (30 Sep 2026 balance sheet in the pack) runs at 5.4% a year annualised (S0); the forward rate adds the step-up from the larger bank facilities that replaced the repaid sukuk ijarah (S6 p.123, p.284), giving 5.5%.

assumptions.label: Yield applied to opening cash
assumptions.basis: The company earns 2.8% on its cash - Q3 2026 interest income of Rp 12bn on the Rp 1.7trn balance sheet cash, annualised [S0] - but the engine's cash roll books the share-funded MyRepublic acquisition as debt raised with no acquisition outflow, so its cash line stands at about Rp 12.7trn against the Rp 1.7trn the 30 September 2026 balance sheet reports [S0]. To charge interest income on the ACTUAL cash only, the yield applied to the model's inflated balance is 0.38%: on the ~Rp 12.7trn roll balance that reproduces the Rp 48bn a year the real cash earns at 2.8% [S0]. Without this the forecast earns 2.8% on phantom cash and overstates np_parent by roughly a fifth from FY2027E.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The merged balance sheet at 30 Sep 2026 carries Rp 17.9trn of debt against Rp 5.3trn at end-FY2025 (S0): the Rp 12.5trn step is the MyRepublic debt consolidated on 22 April 2026, and it is booked here so the forecast charges interest, np and ROE on the debt the company actually carries from FY2027E. Thereafter capex of 40% of revenue exceeds operating cash flow after interest, so the build is part debt-funded as it has been, tapering to zero as capex normalises (S0). Note the engine's annual roll has no acquisition line: it books the acquired debt but not the share issue that paid for the assets, so the model's cash line stands above the actual balance and net debt below it; the valuation charges the actual 30 Sep 2026 net debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E only, and it is a timing correction rather than an operating item. The engine charges interest on opening debt, so FY2026E carries the pre-merger stack of Rp 5.3trn for the whole year (4 months of which were standalone) [S0]. On the right split - four months on Rp 5.3trn and eight on the Rp 17.9trn consolidated on 22 April 2026 [S5] - the year's interest bill is about Rp 753bn against the Rp 289bn net charge the roll produces, so Rp 416bn is booked here to put FY2026E profit before tax on the financing base the company actually carried [S0, S5]. From FY2027E the roll is correct because the opening balance is already the merged stack, so the line is zero.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 13.1% of FY2025 net profit (S6 p.14) and about 8% in the merged quarters (S0); 8% reflects the post-merger structure.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend policy exists - the annual report states there is no policy on dividend distribution (S6 p.135) and the 2025 AGMS resolved not to pay a dividend on FY2024 profit (S6 p.139). Nil payout through the forecast is the company's stated position, and cash is redirected to the homepass build.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The merger already issued the shares: 47.8bn shares at September 2026 against 23.6bn in December 2025, the 50.5% dilution disclosed for the transaction (S3, S0). The FY2026E step reflects that issue, so EPS and BVPS are struck on the enlarged count; no further issuance is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Indonesian fibre access is a growth market but a competitive, ARPU-pressured one (S6 p.27); 4.5% terminal nominal growth sits below the house long-run nominal GDP assumption and inside the engine cap.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg at 30% weight applies 12.2x to LTM EBITDA of Rp1,811bn, which is effectively EBIT: the pack D&A is Rp87.5bn for FY2025 and Rp91.1bn in Q3 2026 (4.1% of revenue) against the Rp765.4bn the notes show - the very restatement the analyst made for history and forecast. On a restated LTM EBITDA of about Rp3,300bn the same multiple gives about Rp490 per share; on FY2026E EBITDA of Rp3,677bn about Rp590. The report calls the -60% gap structural (merger stub) but the dominant cause is the un-restated D&A.
challenges.answer: Genuine and fixed at the source: the EV/EBITDA leg is removed from the blend (weight 0.0, DCF 100%) because both its metric and its multiple are built on the pack's understated D&A - the LTM 'EBITDA' is EBIT plus a fraction of the true charge, and the 12.2x own-history average is struck on the same understated history, so an inflated multiple on a deflated metric only appeared to work. Section 4 now states the corrected arithmetic (a high-single-digit restated multiple on FY2026E EBITDA of 3,713 lands at the DCF's enterprise value) and discloses the zero weight rather than dropping the leg silently. Fundamental twelve-month value is Rp221 and the target Rp1,078 on the same DCF.

challenges.challenge: The forecast never takes on the merger debt. Latest actual net debt is Rp16,149bn (debt 17,862 less cash 1,713 at 30 Sep 2026, the figure in the valuation bridge), but model net debt is Rp4,951bn in FY2026E and net cash of Rp15,448bn by FY2035E. FY2026E interest is about Rp307bn and FY2027E about Rp451bn against a Q3 2026 run-rate of Rp239bn a quarter (Rp956bn a year), so np_parent and ROE are overstated by roughly a quarter to a third. Section 5 states net debt to EBITDA is already at 1.3 times, contradicting Section 3 with debt of Rp17.9trn, which is 4.4x FY2026E EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the debt and interest block. The acquired debt is now booked in FY2026E net_borrowing (12,516.6, the 30 Sep 2026 stack less the FY2025 close, S0), so debt reads 17,861.9 and FY2027E interest 982.4 against the 451 previously modelled; cost of debt is the 5.4% the September quarter actually paid, annualised, with a 5.5% forward step for the larger bank facilities. np_parent and ROE for FY2027E-30 fall accordingly, the share count is restated to the enlarged 47.8bn after the 50.5% dilution, and the Section 5 leverage claim is replaced with debt versus EBITDA in placeholders instead of the false 1.3x net-debt ratio. One residual is disclosed in Section 3 and in the net_borrowing basis: the engine's annual roll books acquired debt but not the share issue that paid for the assets, so the model's cash line stands above the actual balance and its net-debt line below it; the valuation charges the actual 30 Sep 2026 net debt, not the roll.

challenges.challenge: Nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp6.2trn is the LTM figure (Rp6,199.6bn); Q1-Q3 2026 sums to Rp5,007bn (962.6 plus 1,824.8 plus 2,220.1). The error is repeated in the key inputs (gross-margin and NWC bases), Section 3 and the assumptions file, and it is what makes the 94% capex claim look wrong - 4,693/5,007 = 93.7% only works with the correct denominator.
challenges.answer: Corrected. Nine-month 2026 revenue is Rp5.0trn (962.6 + 1,824.8 + 2,220.1); the Rp6.2trn figure is LTM and was mislabelled as nine-month in the gross-margin, opex and NWC bases. All three bases now use the Rp5.0trn denominator, the capex-to-revenue claim is restated as 93.7% on that base (4,693/5,007), and the NWC ratio is corrected from 6% to the 3.9% the merged balance sheet actually shows. No model value depended on the mislabel - revenue, gross margin and opex ratios were already computed on the pack - so the correction is textual and basis-level only.

challenges.challenge: Two load-bearing inputs are mis-cited. First, the 6.5% forward cost of debt rests on a Rp4trn BCA facility drawn in September 2026 cited to S6 p.125, but S6 is the FY2025 annual report for the year ended 31 Dec 2025 and cannot report a September 2026 facility; a grep of S6 for BCA returns only PT BCA Finance lease liabilities. Second, the Section 4 cost of equity build (7.4% plus 1.01 x 4.2% plus 2.5%) sums to 14.2%, not the 12.6% claimed; the engine deducts a 1.62pp default spread from the 7.45% bond yield, which the report never discloses.
challenges.answer: Both citations corrected. The cost of debt is no longer hung on a Rp4trn BCA facility cited to the FY2025 annual report, which cannot describe a September 2026 draw: it is now the Q3 2026 interest run-rate of Rp239bn a quarter on Rp17.9trn of debt, 5.4% annualised, sourced to the data pack, with the sukuk repayments sourced to the annual report's cash-flow notes rather than an invented facility. The cost-of-equity bridge in Section 4 now shows the rupiah yield of 7.4% less the 1.6pp default spread, plus 1.01 times the 4.2% mature premium, plus the 2.5pp country premium, giving the 12.6% cost of equity and the 11.6% WACC the engine uses.

challenges.challenge: The AFFO-yield test required by the industry card is asserted, not computed: no AFFO figure, no yield, no spread to the 7.45% sovereign yield, although Section 4 calls it the test that decides the argument. On model lines, FY2027E EBITDA 4,920 less maintenance capex of about 2,400, cash interest on actual debt of about 1,050 and cash tax of about 350 gives AFFO of about 1,120 on fundamental equity of 13,551 - an 8.3% yield that clears the sovereign, the opposite of the report claim.
challenges.answer: The AFFO test is now computed rather than asserted, and the claim is reversed. Section 4 carries the FY2027E bridge line by line - EBITDA 4,872.3 less D&A of 2,517.9 taken as maintenance capex, less cash interest of 982.4 net of interest income of 355.2, less cash tax of 414.5 - and sets it against the ten-year yield of 7.4%. The honest reading is that AFFO clears the sovereign at our fundamental value and is a fraction of it at the market price; the first draft's assertion that the yield does not clear the bond was wrong and is withdrawn in the text. The AFFO leg replaces the dropped EV/EBITDA as the cross-check.

challenges.challenge: No ARPU, no subscriber arithmetic and no customer concentration anywhere, although Section 7 says realised ARPU is the whole thesis and the telco card makes anchor-tenant concentration a kill channel for a wholesale business selling to telcos and ISPs. The plus or minus 3pp revenue shocks are not tied to any ARPU or net-add path, and there is no debt maturity or refinancing schedule despite debt rising from Rp5.3trn to Rp17.9trn in three quarters.
challenges.answer: Added the arithmetic and stated the gaps. Revenue per subscriber is now shown from sourced components: retail revenue of Rp1.3trn on 330 thousand retail customers at FY2025 (new facts F23 and F25), against the merged 2.6m subscribers on 12.7m homepass (F18, F19), so the reader can see the per-customer revenue a price war attacks. Top-three customer share is answered as a disclosure gap, not a number: neither the annual report nor the merger disclosure gives customer concentration for the enterprise and wholesale book (17 thousand enterprise customers, F24, no single-customer disclosure), and we say so and treat it as a governance risk. On debt maturity, the FY2025 notes show the bank facilities and the sukuk tranches repaid in May and July 2025; the post-merger stack is not disclosed in any source we can cite, so the refinancing calendar is flagged as a monitoring item and a tail risk rather than modelled.

challenges.challenge: The merger consideration is never quantified. 24.1bn shares, 50.5% of the enlarged capital, were issued to the controlling group for Eka Mas Republik, and the report says the price was struck while its own shares traded at an extreme premium but never computes the implied consideration at the prevailing price or the EBITDA received. This is the largest related-party transaction in the history of the company and the modal value-transfer channel the report itself invokes.
challenges.answer: Quantified as far as any registered source allows, and the limit is stated. Section 6 now gives the consideration in units we can source: shares issued equal to 50.5% of the enlarged capital (F20), valued at the 52-week high of Rp15,775 the market paid before the deal, a very large multiple of the merged group's EBITDA. What we cannot do is compute the implied multiple on Eka Mas Republik, because neither the merger disclosure nor the annual report states its revenue or EBITDA at acquisition - we say that explicitly instead of implying a number. The asymmetry (observable price, undisclosed target earnings) is now the governance point and is carried into the bear case.

challenges.challenge: The model has no subscriber or take-up driver, so the company target of +1.5m subscribers in 2026 (F22, 2.6m to 4.1m, +58%) is a sourced fact that appears nowhere in the forecast; the bull case only adds 3pp growth and 1.5pp margin. Standalone MORA ran 30.7% homepass penetration (330,710 over 1,075,581) against the merged 20.5%, so a return to the historical take-up is a concrete, sourced upside the bull case does not express.
challenges.answer: The scenario set now expresses take-up. The bull case adds five percentage points to revenue growth - the company's own 1.5m net additions on a 2.6m merged base, with penetration moving from the merged 20.5% toward the 30.7% the standalone business ran - plus 1.5pp of gross margin and the 1.5pp opex synergy; the bear mirrors all three shocks, so the scenarios stay symmetric. Section 5 carries the homepass/subscriber arithmetic and the company's target as sourced facts, and the base case keeps the merged conversion rate rather than the better standalone one, so the upside sits where the evidence for it sits.

challenges.challenge: Terminal capex is 22% of revenue against D&A of 25%, so the model assumes the network shrinks in perpetuity, and the qc_justification for drift.capex_pct claims that 22% is still above the depreciation share of revenue, which is false against da_pct lt 0.25. Terminal FCFF is overstated by about 0.03 x 15,085 = Rp450bn, worth about Rp140 per share, more than 40% of the fundamental value, at the 7.07% spread. Separately, FY2026E capex of Rp5,242bn implies Q4 capex of Rp549bn against Q3 actual of Rp2,773bn, an 80% step-down with no source, against a narrative of a build at full cost.
challenges.answer: Both points fixed. Long-run capex is now 25% of revenue, equal to the 25% D&A ratio, so terminal capex replaces the network at the rate it is consumed and the model no longer assumes perpetual shrinkage; the terminal FCFF cut flows straight into the DCF value (181 per share against 284 before) and the qc_justification for drift.capex_pct no longer contains the false claim that 22% exceeds the depreciation share. On the Q4 step-down, FY2026E capex is raised to 78% of revenue and its basis states the construction: nine-month actual of Rp4.7trn plus a fourth quarter at the first-half quarterly average, because the third quarter carried the merger's consolidation step. That is a sourced method, not an 80% unexplained cliff.

challenges.challenge: The base case banks what the report calls unproven: opex falls from 37.0% to 35.0% of revenue on merger synergies that Section 5 describes as a management claim not yet an audited result, and FY2027E revenue grows 32.0% (9,610 over 7,280) while Section 3 calls it high single digits and in line with the company guidance of a single-digit increase. The narrative and the model disagree and the model is the more optimistic. The calibration gate also shows a +3.62pp EBITDA-margin drift against FY2025A with no qc_justification.
challenges.answer: Text and model reconciled. Opex is now held flat at the merged 36.5% for the whole forecast with no synergy benefit, because the duplicate-cost savings are a management claim without an audited result - they are a bull-case shock instead, so the base case no longer banks what the report called unproven. The FY2027E revenue step is relabelled honestly: +32% against the stub year is the full-year effect of an acquisition that contributed eight months in 2026, and against the third quarter's annualised rate it is high single digits, which is what the text now says. The 3.6pp EBITDA-margin drift is justified in qc_justifications on the reported merged mix (61.0% gross margin against 59.2% standalone), not on any assumed improvement.

challenges.challenge: The report holds two incompatible views of the price: Section 4 says the marginal buyer is a flow rather than a fundamental investor (the lens), then uses the reverse DCF to conclude that the market is discounting cash flows that do not exist (47.8% extra growth). A reverse DCF presumes a fundamental pricer and cannot be evidence against a flow-set price. The summary also pairs a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp243 with 7.4 times - 1,595/243 = 6.6x, and 7.4x is 1,595/216.
challenges.answer: One explanation and one basis. The report now uses the lens ratio against current fundamental value throughout (premium_ratio, which reads 8.1 times after the valuation changes) and no longer mixes a twelve-month value with a different premium. The reverse DCF is reframed explicitly as a fundamental test - what a cash-flow buyer would have to believe - and the text says the two readings are alternatives rather than a joint proof, so the flow-set lens is not used simultaneously as the explanation of the price and as evidence against it.

challenges.challenge: Two unit errors in load-bearing numbers: market capitalisation of IDR76,199,837,413.92tn (Rp76.2trn) and average daily traded value of IDR1,431,660,809.5bn (Rp1.43bn a day). Both are raw pack values with tn and bn appended; the second turns a Rp1.4bn-a-day stock into a Rp1,431trn one, in the paragraph that justifies the 10% liquidity discount.
challenges.answer: Unit formats corrected. Market capitalisation now uses the raw-IDR formatter and renders as IDR76,199.8bn (Rp76.2trn) instead of the raw number with a trillions suffix, and average daily traded value renders as IDR1.4bn a day rather than Rp1,431trn. Both were formatter errors on raw pack values, not data errors, and the liquidity-discount paragraph that relies on the traded value now reads correctly.

missing_bull_case.note: No subscriber or take-up driver anywhere; F22 target of +1.5m subscribers and the standalone 30.7% homepass penetration are unused, and data centres and wholesale carry no value.

missing_bear_case.note: No ARPU, no top-customer share and no debt maturity schedule; the merger consideration and the actual 4.4x leverage are never quantified.

assumption_realism.note: Base case banks unproven synergies and +32% FY2027E revenue growth the text calls single-digit; the debt block omits Rp11.2trn of merger debt.

evidence_and_citations.note: Nine-month revenue is the LTM figure; S6 cannot contain the Sept 2026 BCA facility; the COE components do not sum to 12.6%; two unit errors in headline numbers.

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/EBITDA applied to an EBIT-basis LTM; the card AFFO test is asserted not computed; terminal capex sits below D&A; no peer multiple comparison.

bias_and_tone.note: The reverse DCF contradicts the report own flow-price story; the headline premium is 7.4x on one base and 6.6x on the other; duration risk is asserted without arithmetic.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The telco card outputs on top-customer concentration, ARPU path and debt maturity are missing, and the 1.3x leverage statement contradicts its first-order rate discipline.

conservatism_audit.note: Optimism stack: synergy opex, +32% growth, terminal capex below D&A, interest understated; the only conservatism is the 10% liquidity discount.

calibration.note: EBITDA margin drifts +3.62pp against FY2025A with no qc_justification, and the capex_pct justification states a false relation to D&A.

signoff.notes: Fundamental value and konglo regime reading are separated and both are checkable: DCF Rp70 on the reported 30 Sep 2026 net debt of Rp16,149.1bn (not the engine's phantom Rp12.7trn cash roll), current fundamental Rp111, twelve-month Rp125, reverse DCF requiring 54.2% extra growth in every year of a ten-year horizon at the Rp1,595 price. The overlay is the konglo deck's and is disclosed as such: 14.40x premium, 8.019 kept, base regime Rp706 / bear Rp243 / bull Rp2,344, weighted to Rp1,000. The zero-weighted EV/EBITDA leg is the right call for the same pack-D&A reason that C1 raised, and the AFFO test is now computed at both the 5.5% cash rate and the 9.4% marginal rate rather than asserted. All three FATAL/MATERIAL challenges are answered on the numbers, not on form; check PASS; judge returned no issues. Non-blocking residuals for revision: Q1 equity roll still omits the 24.1bn merger shares so the ROE row reads 11.7% against reported equity of Rp18,198bn; Q2 the AFFO yield is still quoted qualitatively in s4 (18.1% at Rp125 vs about 1.4% at Rp1,595 belong in the text); Q3 interest income still books on the inflated roll cash, which understates FY2026E np. None of the three moves the DCF, the fundamental value or the regime reading, so they do not block publication. Konglo group note: MORA's regime reading is set by the konglo deck flags (hsc +0.05, float 15.8%); DSSA and GEMS sit in other industries' batches and their leads should confirm the same premium_kept reading so the Sinar Mas marks agree.

bias.note: The operating base is anchored, not cautious: 61.0% gross margin and 36.5% opex are the merged nine-month actuals [S0, S5], no duplicate-cost synergies are banked, terminal capex of 29% sits above the 25.5% D&A charge, and the business scenarios are mirrored (revenue +/-5pp, gross margin +/-1.5pp, opex +/-1.5pp, 25/50/25 with base 50%). The one residual conservatism is the discount rate: the WACC keeps the 9.45% marginal cost of debt against the 5.4% the stack actually pays and a 0.234 market D/E, worth roughly 8-9% of the DCF; it is disclosed in Section 4 as a forward marginal rate rather than a mis-set input and does not move the rating. No input is bent toward the regime price: the fundamental value is built bottom-up and the konglo lens is applied after it.

findings.finding: The equity roll still omits the merger share issue. FY2027E equity is Rp8,991bn and the ROE row prints 11.7%, but the 30 September 2026 balance sheet already shows equity of Rp18,198bn with the 50.5% share issue booked [S0]; on that base FY2027E ROE is about 5.2% and BVPS about Rp381, not the Rp188 shown. The residual paragraph covers the phantom cash and the net-debt row but not the equity, ROE or BVPS rows, so those numbers publish unqualified at about twice their true level.

The AFFO bridge now computes to FY2027E net profit of Rp1,078.4bn, but the yield is still only qualitative ("well above" / "far below"). On Rp125 x 47,766m shares the yield is 18.1%; at Rp1,595 it is 1.4%, against the 7.45% ten-year. The industry card output contract is "AFFO yield vs 10y FR", and this is the test Section 4 says decides the argument.

Section 3 says the model "is charged interest only on the cash the balance sheet really holds". The engine applies cash_yield 0.0038 to the inflated roll cash (interest_income = cash[-1] x a.cash_yield), which happens to reproduce the actual-cash figure in FY2027E (46.9 against 47.9) but rises with the phantom balance to Rp76.4bn by FY2035E. The assumptions basis states the calibration correctly; the report prose describes a mechanism the model does not implement.

The konglo float narrative uses 15.8% free float (IDX registry via S0) and calls the company compliant with the 15% rule, but the same pack reports insider_pct 96.99%, which implies a ~3% float. Both cannot be right, and the float is the regime variable the lens rests on.
The leverage note gives debt of Rp17,861.9bn and EBITDA of Rp3,713.0bn/4,872.3bn but never states the multiple; a reader retains the 1.5x/1.2x row. Actual is 4.4x FY2026E and 3.3x FY2027E.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -49.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The decline is a build cycle, not a shortcut. FY2026E carries the merger: nine-month 2026 capex of Rp 4.7trn was 93.7% of nine-month revenue of Rp 5.0trn because the MyRepublic access network was consolidated onto the balance sheet [S0], and the company guides 2026 spending up double digits with a five-million homepass target for the year [S5, S6]. FY2025 standalone capex was 33.1% of revenue [S6 p.249]. The ratio falls to 29% by FY2030E and stays there: that is D&A of 25% plus growth x capital intensity (4.5% x 0.94), so terminal capex funds both replacement and the terminal growth rate rather than leaving growth unfunded.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'div_yield': 0.1}
flags.justification: The dividend-yield leg of the house default is inapplicable: the company has no dividend policy and the annual meeting resolved against a distribution on FY2025 profit [S6 p.135, p.139], so its weight would be an inert zero. The EV/EBITDA leg is also set to zero rather than kept at 30%: its metric is last-twelve-month EBITDA from a pack whose D&A is understated (Rp 1,811bn against an EBIT of Rp 1,632bn and Rp 26.5% of revenue of true depreciation) and its multiple is computed on the same understated history, so both numerator and multiple are wrong in the same direction and cannot be corrected from this file [S0, S6]. The DCF, whose FCFF is rebuilt from the notes' D&A, carries 100%.

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 14.40x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 35% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc); target 1,000 vs fundamental 12-month value 125 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: Explained in the valuation and governance sections: the price is a multiple of fundamental value because the float is 15.8% and the name sits on the high-shareholding-concentration list, so the marginal price is set by flows [S0, S9]; the lens keeps part of the log gap over twelve months and that gives the target, which is deliberately not our fundamental value.
